keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (no Cliopatria row; its Han Dynasty shape reaches 128E and contains the coast). The page says only 'the northern Korean Peninsula' (107 BCE) and that North Korean and some South Korean scholars place Xuantu outside the peninsula, in Shenyang, a view not accepted in US, Chinese or Japanese academia. The east coast reading rests on Bowman, quoted on the Lintun page. No area is given anywhere.

region.text: Xuantu's first seat, 'Fort Okjeo': the page says only 'the northern Korean Peninsula'; the Lintun page quotes Bowman that 'Lintun and originally Xuantu were centered on the east coast of northern Korea'

ledger.note: 107 BCE: the Han found Xuantu after the conquest of Wiman Joseon. 'established in 107 BCE in the northern Korean Peninsula'; Four Commanderies page: 'in the place of Gojoseon's ally, Yemaek'. Seat Fort Okjeo; the east-coast placement is Bowman's, quoted on the Lintun page.

region.text: the Lintun prefectures left after 82 BCE (new Dongyi at Wonsan, Buer at Anbyon)

ledger.note: 82 BCE: Lintun is merged into Xuantu. 'In 82 BCE, Lintun was absorbed into Xuantu' (Four Commanderies page). The Lintun page's own text instead has seven prefectures incorporated into Lelang that year; only the Wonsan-Anbyon remnant is drawn.

75 BCE: Xuantu's seat leaves Fort Okjeo. 'In 75 BC, the seat moved from Fort Okjeo to Gaogouli County ... due to raids by the Maek tribes'; the same page says it 'moved its capital to Liaodong in 75 BC due to native resistance'.

region.text: the Lintun prefectures left after 82 BCE (new Dongyi at Wonsan, Buer at Anbyon)

ledger.note: 75 BCE: the Lintun remnant goes to Lelang. 'Lintun was transferred to Lelang in 75 BCE' (Four Commanderies page, Lintun section).

region.text: Xuantu's first seat, 'Fort Okjeo': the page says only 'the northern Korean Peninsula'; the Lintun page quotes Bowman that 'Lintun and originally Xuantu were centered on the east coast of northern Korea'

ledger.note: 75 BCE: the Korean coast is left behind. The page says the seat moved west because of 'raids by the Maek tribes' and 'native resistance' but not who held the Hamgyong coast afterwards; the dong-okjeo dossier (jk-02-a) has the Okjeo as a separate polity from -36. Bridging judgment.

region.text: Gaogouli County, the seat after 75 BCE: 'most probably in the Tonghua region of Manchuria' (Bowman, Lintun page); three counties remained: Gaogouli, Shangyintai, Xigaima

ledger.note: 75 BCE: Xuantu is rebuilt around Gaogouli County in the Tonghua region (Bowman via the Lintun page); the page names three counties (Gaogouli, Shangyintai, Xigaima) and no land. Counterpart nobody because no state is named on the pages.

204: Xuantu falls under the Gongsun of Liaodong. Gongsun Kang page: 'In 204, he inherited his father's appointment and controlled the territories of Liaodong, Xuantu and Lelang commanderies.' The commandery keeps its name; the metropole tint passes to gongsun-liaodong.
238: Wei conquers Xuantu with the Gongsun. 'Sima Yi of Cao Wei conquered Gongsun Yuan in his military campaign against Liaodong in 238.' The metropole becomes cao-wei.

238: the commandery retreats to Fushun. 'four counties remained in the new Xuantu, which had retreated west to present-day Fushun.' The page does not date the retreat; the Wei conquest is used as the bridging year.

265: Xuantu passes to the Jin. The Four Commanderies page says the region was 'ruled by Cao Wei, Jin, and the Murong Xianbei' until 319 without years; the start of Cliopatria's Western Jin is a bridge.

region.text: the 'new Xuantu, which had retreated west to present-day Fushun', four counties

ledger.note: 319: Goguryeo conquers Xuantu. 'Xuantu was conquered by Goguryeo in 319 CE.' The goguryeo dossier has no matching gain event (see notes).

region.text: the 'new Xuantu, which had retreated west to present-day Fushun', four counties

ledger.note: 319: the last Han commandery in Manchuria ends (Four Commanderies page: '107 BCE-319 CE').

wars.name: Buyeo attacks on Xuantu
wars.outcome: Buyeo is an Eastern Han ally: 'c. 122: Buyeo sent troops to the Xuantu Commandery to help against Goguryeo'; 'in 167 Buyeo attacked Xuantu and was defeated' (Buyeo page); in 111 it attacked some Eastern Han holdings.
wars.note: No border moved; Goguryeo's own border wars with Han Liaodong (105-146) are on the Taejo page (goguryeo dossier), not on the Xuantu page.

wars.name: Goguryeo-Wei War
wars.outcome: Cao Wei victory: Guanqiu Jian 'set out from Xuantu Commandery into Goguryeo with seven legions' and Wang Qi, grand administrator of Xuantu, pursued King Dongcheon into the Okjeo lands.
wars.note: Xuantu was the base of the Wei attack; no Xuantu land changed hands.

certainty.note: The pages give counties and seats but no boundaries; the first location is disputed (peninsula or Shenyang), and the post-75 BCE seat is 'most probably' Tonghua.

notes: Colony dossier; no Cliopatria row (Han, Xin, Cao Wei, Western Jin shapes contain the Korean-coast years only; after 75 BCE the commandery sits in Manchuria, possibly partly under Cliopatria's Han shapes, whose bounding box reaches 42.8N). Three placements are readings: the first seat (Hamgyong coast, Bowman via the Lintun page; the Xuantu page itself says only 'the northern Korean Peninsula' and records a rival Shenyang theory), the Gaogouli seat (Tonghua) and the Fushun retreat. The Xuantu page contradicts itself on the 75 BCE move (Gaogouli County versus Liaodong). Not on any page opened: Goguryeo's border wars with Han Liaodong in 105-146 (the Taejo page, in the goguryeo dossier), the Murong Xianbei period before 319, the exact year of the Fushun retreat. Counterparts needing a dossier: lintun-commandery (written), gongsun-liaodong (this batch), buyeo (this batch).
